claims.text: The hypothesis applies to as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Microstructure governs the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of these alloys.
Magnetic properties govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of these alloys.
Thermal-processing history governs the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of these alloys.
The operative microstructural mediators include grain size, phase distribution, and defects.
The interplay among magnetic properties, microstructure, and thermal-processing history influences the magnetostructural transition.
Changes in the magnetostructural transition determine the resulting magnetocaloric response.
Alloy composition can alter magnetocaloric performance.
An optimized microstructure and composition will enhance the magnetocaloric response relative to the as-deposited baseline.
An optimized microstructure and composition will reduce hysteresis relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Impurities, defects, and interface effects may also influence the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
The predictions are intended to hold within the unspecified limits of microstructural and compositional variation achievable by thermal processing and alloy design.
The proposed experiment varies both thermal processing and alloy composition while measuring magnetization, entropy change, and hysteresis loops.
Failure of the nominally optimized material to show both enhanced magnetocaloric response and reduced hysteresis would falsify the hypothesis.
